evidence.claim: Video uploading flow involves original blob storage, transcoding servers, transcoded storage, CDN caching, metadata database, cache, and completion queue with handlers.
Video streaming flow streams video directly from CDN edge servers supporting adaptive streaming protocols.
Metadata is sharded and replicated for performance and high availability, with caching to improve read performance.
Video transcoding pipelines can be modeled as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG) to allow flexible and parallel processing.
Leveraging existing cloud services like blob storage and CDN is recommended to reduce complexity and cost.

research.research_summary: For a large-scale video upload/playback system, the strongest primary-source-backed design choices are: (1) use adaptive bitrate streaming with HLS and/or MPEG-DASH, preferably CMAF-packaged segments so a single encoded asset can serve multiple playback paths; Apple documents HLS support for multiple bitrate tiers, intelligent switching on bandwidth changes, and CMAF support on modern Apple platforms, while DASH-IF documents CMAF media profiles and codec signaling. (2) Build an explicit encoding ladder rather than a single output: authoritative cloud guidance shows common production codecs include AVC/H.264, HEVC/H.265, and AV1, with vendor-specific max output resolutions and recommended encoding settings; Apple’s HLS authoring spec notes that multiple streams should cover anticipated bandwidths. (3) Use multipart upload for large source files so interrupted uploads can retry only failed parts instead of restarting, and pair it with checksum validation and object versioning. (4) Encrypt stored media with cloud object encryption plus streaming encryption/DRM; for delivery, HLS/CMAF commonly uses cbcs or AES-128/SAMPLE-AES variants, and Google Cloud’s live-stream docs explicitly distinguish encryption schemes by protocol/container/DRM. (5) For delivery cost and latency, CloudFront guidance recommends increasing cache hit ratio and using Origin Shield; this directly supports the usual strategy of edge caching popular renditions and minimizing origin fetches. (6) For transcoding workflows, cloud transcoder systems expose explicit job limits and IAM-based access control; the interview-style DAG scheduler concept is consistent with these managed pipeline semantics, but the exact DAG implementation details are an architectural choice rather than a standard. (7) For observability, the primary sources here do not prescribe a single monitoring stack, but the operational implication is to instrument upload completion, transcode job stages, CDN hit ratio, error rates, and queue lag because those are the critical control points exposed by the upload/transcode/CDN model. There is still uncertainty on the exact optimal bitrate ladder, codec mix, and client compatibility matrix because those depend on target devices, content type, and product constraints; the sources support the framework, not a one-size-fits-all ladder.
